questions.q: Trace the development of the Mughal school of painting under Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan.
answer: The Mughal school of miniature painting was a court art that blended Persian, Indian and later European styles, and it developed distinctively under three great emperors.

answer.text: Though begun under Humayun, who brought Persian masters, the school truly flourished under Akbar. He set up a large imperial atelier where artists like Daswanth and Basawan illustrated great manuscripts such as the Hamzanama, Akbarnama and Razmnama. The style was vigorous, colourful and full of crowded, lively scenes.

Jahangir, a keen connoisseur, encouraged fine naturalism and portraiture. Masters like Ustad Mansur painted birds, animals and flowers with great accuracy, and European influence brought shading and allegory.
Under Shah Jahan painting became more formal, refined and jewel-like, with elegant court scenes and lavish use of gold.

answer: Thus Mughal painting evolved from energetic narrative under Akbar to refined elegance under Shah Jahan.

questions.q: What were the defining characteristics of Mughal miniature painting?

answer.text: grew in the imperial workshops and blended Persian, Indian and later European elements into a rich, distinctive style.

list: It is marked by fine detail, delicate brushwork and a rich use of colour and gold
It used naturalism and depth, showing figures and landscapes realistically
It depicted court scenes, battles, portraits, and the histories of the emperors in illustrated chronicles
Under Jahangir it excelled in lifelike portraits and studies of birds, animals and flowers

questions.q: How did European contact influence Mughal painting?

answer.text: contact with Europeans, especially through Jesuit missionaries who brought European prints and paintings, influenced Mughal art.

list: Mughal artists studied and copied European works brought to the court
They adopted new techniques of shading and perspective to give figures roundness and depth

answer.text: Indian and European ideas were fused.

list: Artists learned to model faces with light and shade and to suggest distance in landscapes
European motifs like halos and certain poses entered Mughal painting, while the Indian love of colour and detail remained
